name: Zephaniah

overview.author: Zephaniah son of Cushi, a descendant of King Hezekiah (1:1).
overview.date: During the reign of Josiah (640–609 BC), likely before Josiah’s reforms of 622 BC.
overview.audience: Judah and Jerusalem, along with surrounding nations.
overview.setting: After the wicked reigns of Manasseh and Amon, Judah was filled with Baal worship, astrology, and complacency.
overview.purpose: To warn of the coming day of the LORD on Judah and the nations, call the humble to seek God, and promise a purified remnant in whom God delights.
overview.structure: The day of the LORD against Judah (1), a call to repentance and judgment on the nations (2), and judgment on Jerusalem followed by restoration and joy (3).

items.title: Judgment on all the earth and Judah
A purified people and a rejoicing God

themes.title: The Day of the LORD
themes.text: A great and bitter day of wrath on sin, near and hastening fast.

themes.title: Complacency
themes.text: God punishes those who say, “The LORD will not do good, nor will he do ill” (1:12).

themes.title: Humility
themes.text: “Seek the LORD, all you humble of the land” (2:3).

themes.title: Universal Judgment
themes.text: Nations around Judah are judged as well.

themes.title: The Remnant
themes.text: God leaves a humble and lowly people who seek refuge in Him.

themes.title: God’s Joy
themes.text: “He will rejoice over you with gladness... he will exult over you with loud singing” (3:17).

keyVerses.quote: The great day of the LORD is near, near and hastening fast.
Seek the LORD, all you humble of the land.
The LORD your God is in your midst, a mighty one who will save.
He will rejoice over you with gladness.

christInBook.text: “The King of Israel, the LORD, is in your midst” is fulfilled in Jesus, King of Israel (John 1:49; 12:13).
God giving the peoples pure speech to call on His name anticipates Pentecost (Acts 2).
The mighty one who saves and rejoices over His people is revealed in Christ (Luke 15:7).

crossReferences.note: Rejoicing in heaven over sinners who repent.

reflection: Where might complacency (1:12) have crept into your relationship with God?
What does it mean to “seek humility” (2:3)?
How does the image of God singing over you (3:17) affect you?
How does Zephaniah’s message prepare us for the day of the Lord?
What shame (3:19) do you need to trust God to turn into praise?

chapterList.title: The Great Day of the LORD
chapterList.summary: God will sweep away everything from the face of the earth. Judah is judged for worshiping Baal, the starry host, and Milcom, and for complacency. “The great day of the LORD is near... a day of wrath... a day of darkness.” Silver and gold cannot deliver them.
questions: What idolatry and complacency does God condemn (1:4–6, 12)?
How does Zephaniah describe the day of the LORD (1:14–16)?

chapterList.title: Seek the LORD, You Humble
chapterList.summary: Zephaniah calls the shameless nation to gather before the decree. “Seek the LORD, all you humble of the land... seek righteousness; seek humility; perhaps you may be hidden on the day of the anger of the LORD.” Judgment falls on Philistia, Moab, Ammon, Cush, and Assyria. Nineveh will become desolate.
questions: What three things are the humble to seek (2:3)?
Why are Moab and Ammon judged (2:8–10)?
How did Nineveh’s pride (2:15) lead to its fall?

chapterList.title: The LORD Rejoices Over You
chapterList.summary: Jerusalem is a rebellious, oppressive city whose leaders are corrupt. But God will change the speech of peoples so they call on His name, and leave a humble remnant. “Sing aloud, O daughter of Zion!... The LORD your God is in your midst, a mighty one who will save; he will rejoice over you with gladness... he will exult over you with loud singing.” He will gather the outcasts and change their shame into praise.
questions: What does 3:17 tell you about how God feels toward His people?
What does God promise the lame and outcast (3:19–20)?

tagline: The great day of the LORD, and the God who sings over His people
readingPlan: 3 chapters: one chapter a day takes 3 days; two a day takes about 2 days. For each chapter, read it on ESV.org, then come back here for the summary, questions, and your notes.
